ʻAnini Beach
Kauaʻi's largest reef creates a protected lagoon. Best snorkel at mid-to-high tide.
Small lot off Anini Rd. Fills fast on weekends — arrive before 8am.
9am–5:30pm seasonal
Poʻipū Beach Park
Lifeguarded, sandy entry, reef protection. Hawaiian monk seals haul out here — give them 50ft of space.
Free parking lot adjacent to beach. Busy weekends — arrive early.
9am–5:30pm daily
Salt Pond Beach
Kauaʻi's best-kept secret. Two protected coves, very calm water. Best sunset on the west side.
Large county park lot — rarely full. Restrooms and showers on site.
10am–5pm seasonal
Hanalei Bay
2-mile crescent backed by Nā Pali mountains. Closes for swimming Nov–Mar. River mouth = brown water after rain.
Black Pot Beach lot fills by 8am on weekends. Overflow parking on Weke Rd.
Lydgate Beach Park
Stone breakwater creates the most protected lagoon on the east side. Perfect for first-time snorkelers.
Large free lot — easiest beach access on the east side.
Keʻe Beach
End of the road. Raised reef lagoon, excellent visibility. Summer only — if surf breaks over the reef, don't enter. Parking permit required.
Permit required — book via gostateparks.hawaii.gov. No permit, no entry. Book weeks in advance.
9am–5pm seasonal
Queen's Bath
Lava ledge — not a beach. Waves sweep the shelf year-round. Multiple fatalities. Summer flat conditions only.
Roadside parking on Punahele Rd. 15-min walk to ledge.
Brennecke Beach

Famous for body surfing — but the shorebreak that draws skilled riders has injured many visitors. The break dumps directly onto sand at a steep angle. Watch from shore; swim at Poʻipū next door instead.
Steep, dumping shorebreak directly onto hard sand. Severe neck and back injuries reported regularly. Bodyboard/surf only if you have local-equivalent experience; otherwise watch from shore.
Shared lot with Poipu Beach Park.
Lumahaʻi Beach
Stunning to photograph from shore. Do not swim here, ever.
"Luma-die" — strong shorebreak and currents. Multiple drownings. No safe entry.
Roadside pullouts on Kūhiō Hwy.
No lifeguard
Secret Beach (Kauapea)
Spectacular views but enter water only on calmest summer days.
No lifeguard, strong currents, 2 deaths. Unguarded waterfall area dangerous.

Kalihiwai Bay
Locals only spot. Watch the stream mouth carefully if entering.
Stream mouth has strong currents. Surf can pick up suddenly. No lifeguard.
Small lot at end of Kalihiwai Rd.
Polihale State Park
Spectacular sunset and stargazing — but stay out of the water entirely.
Brutal shorebreak, no lifeguard, 5+ deaths. Treacherous all year.
5-mile dirt road, 4WD only. No facilities.
Kōloa Landing

Popular shore dive but ROPE deaths in 2023-2024. Calm water can mask danger.
Public lot at end of Hoonani Rd.
Tunnels (Mākua)
Best snorkel on the north shore in summer. Dangerous in winter — channels become exit rips.
Limited roadside spots on Kuhio Hwy. Walk in via Haena State Park lot.
No lifeguard — closest at Haena
Keālia Beach
Long sandy stretch good for walking. Strong shorebreak — body surfers only.
Large paved lot off Kuhio Hwy. Restrooms.
9am–5pm daily
Kalapakī Beach
Wheelchair-accessible beach. Calm protected bay great for kids and beginners.
Marriott resort lot — beach is public. Paved path to sand.
Māhāʻulepū Beach
Wild and undeveloped — walk the heritage trail along the cliffs. Watch for monk seals.
Dirt road past Grand Hyatt. 4WD helpful but not required in dry weather.
Wailua Beach
River meets ocean here — currents at the mouth. Good for picnics on the sand.
Roadside on Kuhio Hwy.
Kekaha Beach Park
Long sandy stretch on the west side. Strong currents most of the year — swim only when calm and lifeguards confirm. Sunsets here are exceptional.
Pakala (Infinities)
Famous left point break for experienced surfers. Long walk in from Hwy 50. Not a swim beach — rocky, currents, no lifeguard.
Shipwreck Beach (Keoneloa)

Iconic Grand Hyatt-adjacent beach with the dramatic cliff (Makawehi) at the east end. Strong shorebreak — bodyboarders only, watch from shore otherwise. Sunrise walk to the lithified dunes is the move.
Donkey Beach (Paliku)
10-minute walk down from the highway pullout north of Kapaʻa. Often empty. Strong currents, occasional clothing-optional users. Worth it for solitude and the cliffside trail.
Kāʻanapali Beach

Long, calm leeward beach in summer; the gentlest swimming is at the south/central stretch. There is NO lifeguard — Kāʻanapali has among the most snorkel-related drownings in Hawaiʻi, with strong currents concentrated near the Black Rock point. Stay close to shore, never snorkel alone, and check the daily flag; surf and shorebreak build in winter.

No lifeguard on the main resort beach. Kāʻanapali (especially toward the Black Rock point) is one of Hawaiʻi's deadliest snorkeling areas — strong, hard-to-see currents and snorkel-related fatalities are documented. Swim/snorkel near shore on calm days only.
Limited public lots at Whalers Village and beach access points off Kāʻanapali Pkwy — fill by mid-morning. Resort lots are paid/validated.

No county lifeguard — resort beach patrols only; nearest guarded tower is Hanakaʻōʻō (Canoe Beach) at the south end. (County has discussed adding a Kāʻanapali/Black Rock tower, not yet confirmed staffed.)
Puʻu Kekaʻa (Black Rock)

Excellent snorkeling on the calm inside, but a current sweeps around the point and the cliff-jump (lele kawa) at the tip has caused fatal and serious injuries; stay inside the cove on calm days only and do not jump.

Strong current wraps around the lava point and offshore; this is one of Hawaiʻi's highest snorkel-drowning locations. The popular cliff jump at the tip has caused drownings and serious injuries. No lifeguard. Snorkel only inside the cove on calm days, stay close to shore, and do not jump from the rock.
Sheraton Maui lot or Kāʻanapali public beach access — walk north along the sand to the point.
Kahekili Beach Park (Airport Beach)

One of West Maui's best easy-entry snorkel reefs (part of the Kahekili Herbivore Fisheries Reserve); enter from the sandy patches and float over the reef, calmest in the morning. No lifeguard — a current can run in the channel, so avoid drifting far from shore.
Free county lot at Kahekili Beach Park with restrooms, showers and shade — usually space if you arrive before 10am.
Kapalua Bay

Two rocky points shelter this C-shaped crescent into one of Maui's calmest, most family-friendly swim and snorkel bays; reef and turtles are right off the sand. No lifeguard, so still watch the kids and check conditions.
Small free public lot off Lower Honoapiʻilani Rd with restrooms and a beach tunnel — fills very early; arrive before 9am.
Nāpili Bay

A sandy pocket bay with good morning snorkeling at the points and frequent green sea turtles; small shorebreak can form at the center when a south or west swell runs, so enter near the rocks. No lifeguard.
Very limited — a few public beach-access paths between condos off Napili Pl/Hui Dr. Walk in; no dedicated lot.
D.T. Fleming Beach Park

Beautiful guarded beach (one of only two lifeguarded beaches in West Maui), but it faces more north and catches winter and NW swell that build a powerful shorebreak and rip currents — swim near the lifeguard tower and heed the flags. The steep nearshore slope can cause a strong undertow when surf is up.
Free county lot off Honoapiʻilani Hwy with restrooms and showers — generally available.
Approx 8:00am–4:30pm daily (Maui County Ocean Safety)
Honokōwai Beach Park
A shallow, reef-sheltered wading pool that is very calm and good for small children at higher tides; it gets rocky and bottoms out at low tide, so time your visit to the tide. No lifeguard.
Small free county lot at the park off Lower Honoapiʻilani Rd with a grassy lawn, restrooms and showers.
Launiupoko Beach Park

A lava-rock-walled wading pool keeps the water flat and warm for toddlers, while a gentle outside break draws beginner surfers; the West Maui Mountains backdrop makes for great sunset photos. No lifeguard.
Free county lot off Honoapiʻilani Hwy with restrooms and showers — popular but usually has turnover.
Olowalu Beach

Shallow, calm reef known as a turtle-cleaning station, with easy entry — but Olowalu is the ONLY Maui beach with permanent shark-warning signs (a reef-shark pupping ground). Snorkel only in clear water, never at dawn/dusk or after rain when water is murky. The reef is fragile and very shallow — float, never stand, and go at higher tide.

No lifeguard. Olowalu has permanent posted shark-warning signs — it is a known reef-shark pupping ground with elevated shark presence (rare attacks, but real). Avoid murky/turbid water, dawn/dusk, and post-rain runoff. Very shallow coral makes low tide hazardous to swimmers and reef alike.
Roadside dirt pullouts along Honoapiʻilani Hwy near mile-marker 14; no facilities.
Ukumehame Beach Park

A long, shaded sand-and-pebble beach with a beginner surf break offshore (Thousand Peaks); swimming is reasonable on calm days but the bottom drops off and south swells bring shorebreak, so watch conditions. No lifeguard — and this stretch (with Olowalu) sees elevated tiger-shark activity, so avoid murky water and dawn/dusk.
Roadside parking and a small lot along Honoapiʻilani Hwy fronting the kiawe trees; basic facilities.
Honolua Bay

A Marine Life Conservation District with superb summer snorkeling on the right side of the bay — but in winter it becomes a world-class big-wave surf break that is extremely dangerous and off-limits to swimmers. No lifeguard; rocky/boulder entry.

Faces NNW and takes the full force of winter N/NW swell, turning into a powerful big-wave surf break (Oct–Apr) with no lifeguard, strong currents and a rocky/boulder entry. Snorkel here only on calm flat summer days; in winter stay out of the water and watch from the cliff.
Roadside along Honoapiʻilani Hwy near mile-marker 32, then a 5–10 min walk through forest; no facilities.
Mokuleʻia Beach (Slaughterhouse)

A gorgeous pocket beach with good snorkeling and bodysurfing on calm summer days only; the steep stairs, exposed pocket and powerful winter shorebreak make it hazardous much of the year. No lifeguard.

NNW-facing pocket beach in the Honolua–Mokuleʻia Marine Life Conservation District with no lifeguard, steep cliff stairway access and a heavy, dumping shorebreak plus rip currents on any north/NW swell (most of winter). Enter only on flat calm summer days; rescues here are difficult.
Roadside pullouts on Honoapiʻilani Hwy near mile-marker 32, then a steep concrete-and-rock stairway down the cliff; no facilities.
Kamaʻole Beach Park I

The northernmost and most protected of the three Kamaʻole parks. Lifeguarded, sandy entry, gentle in summer — a safe default for families. Still check with the lifeguard, as south swells can bring shorebreak and rip currents.
Free lot at the park plus roadside on S. Kīhei Rd. Fills midday — come before 10am.
8am–4:45pm daily
Kamaʻole Beach Park II

Steeper drop-off than Kam I means slightly stronger shorebreak — fine for swimming when calm, but watch small kids at the waterline. Snorkel the rocky points at each end. Lifeguarded; ask the tower about conditions.
Small lots at both ends plus roadside on S. Kīhei Rd. Tight midday.
Kamaʻole Beach Park III

Grassy park with shade, playground and lifeguards makes this the family pick of the Kamaʻole trio. Shorebreak can dump on a rising south swell — keep toddlers at the shallows and check with the lifeguard.
Largest lot of the three, with a grassy park, restrooms and showers. Easiest South Kīhei parking.
Charley Young Beach

A quieter pocket just north of Kamaʻole I with soft golden sand and turtles on the north reef. No lifeguard here — surf can get rough and rip currents form on south swells; the nearest tower is a short walk south at Kam I, so swim down there with kids if in any doubt.
Tiny lot at the end of Kaiau Pl plus a stairway access off Kīhei Rd. Very limited — arrive early.
No lifeguard — nearest tower at Kamaʻole I
Keawakapu Beach

Long, beautiful golden-sand beach straddling the Kīhei–Wailea line, with good morning swimming and snorkeling off the rocky ends when calm. No lifeguard and a documented drowning history — snorkel only when flat, stay near shore, and never go out alone.

No lifeguard on a long, open beach with documented snorkeling fatalities (a visitor snorkeler drowned here in Aug 2017) and rip currents that strengthen on south swells, especially toward the rocky ends and offshore. Midday trade winds pick up and can push swimmers and snorkelers out. Snorkel only on a calm morning, stay close to shore, never snorkel alone, and judge the surf yourself — there is no one watching the water.
Lots at the north end (Kīhei Rd) and south end (Wailea Alanui). South lot is the better bet for early arrivals.
Mokapu & Ulua Beach

The rocky point between Mokapu and Ulua is one of South Maui's best easy-access snorkel reefs — turtles and reef fish in calm morning water. No lifeguard and a documented drowning here; visibility and safety both drop fast once the trades pick up by midday. Snorkel early, near shore, and never alone.

No lifeguard. A 63-year-old visitor drowned while snorkeling off Mokapu in July 2018, part of a documented pattern of snorkeling deaths on Maui's unguarded south-shore reefs. The popular reef point looks calm in the morning but afternoon trade winds (typically by ~2pm) build chop and current, and water can pull offshore. Snorkel only on a calm morning, stay close to shore, never snorkel alone, and get out when the wind comes up.
Small public lot on Ulua Beach Rd between the Wailea resorts. Fills by 9am with snorkelers.
Wailea Beach

Postcard resort beach with snorkeling off the south point — but it has a serious recent drowning history and NO lifeguard, despite looking calm. Treat the water with respect: swim only when flat, stay near shore, never alone. The paved Wailea coastal walk links it to Ulua and Polo for a safe scenic stroll.

No lifeguard on a beach with a serious recent drowning history. In May 2025 two visitors (a father and son) died in rip-current conditions off Wailea Beach; bystanders, not lifeguards, attempted the rescue. A snorkeler also died here in 2022, and rip-current rescues have recurred over the years. The water looks calm and resort-tame but rip currents form, especially toward the south point and on south swells. Swim or snorkel only when genuinely calm, stay close to shore, never go alone, and if caught in a current don't fight it — float and signal for help.
Public lot off Wailea Alanui between the Four Seasons and Grand Wailea. Limited — go early or walk the coastal path.
Polo Beach

The southern end of Wailea's resort beaches — quieter than Wailea Beach, with snorkeling off the rocks at each end. No lifeguard, and shorebreak/rip currents pick up on south swells on a coast with recent drownings. Enter only when calm and stay near shore.

No lifeguard, on the same Wailea resort coast where multiple visitor drownings have occurred at adjacent unguarded beaches (Wailea Beach, Mokapu). Shorebreak and rip currents pick up on south swells, and there is no one watching the water. Swim or snorkel only when calm, stay close to shore, and never go alone.
Public lot off Kaukahi St below the Fairmont Kea Lani. Usually the easiest Wailea parking.
Maluaka Beach

Known as 'Turtle Town' for the green sea turtles on the south reef — one of Mākena's best snorkels in calm morning water. No lifeguard and a documented drowning here; snorkelers often go too far offshore. Stay near shore, snorkel only when calm, and never go alone.

No lifeguard. A 71-year-old visitor drowned while snorkeling alone off Maluaka ('Turtle Town') in Jan 2018. The reef draws crowds of snorkelers but the water can develop current and chop, and people venture far offshore chasing turtles. Snorkel only on a calm morning, stay close to shore, never snorkel alone, and turn back when the wind builds. Nearest lifeguard is at Makena State Park (Big Beach), not here.
Small lots off Mākena Rd at each end of the beach. Limited — early arrival helps.
Mākena Landing

A rocky shore-dive and kayak launch, not a sandy swim beach — entry is over lava, so water shoes help. Excellent snorkeling north toward the lava points when flat. No lifeguard, rocky entry, and snorkelers range far offshore — for confident swimmers only, on calm mornings, with a buddy.

No lifeguard and NOT a sandy swim beach — entry is over lava rock, so this is a shore-dive and kayak launch for confident swimmers only. It sits within the Mākena 'Turtle Town' reef system, where a visitor snorkeler drowned in Jan 2018; snorkelers here range far offshore toward the lava points and can be caught by current and afternoon wind. Use water shoes, snorkel only on a flat calm morning, stay with a buddy, and turn back when conditions build.
County park lot with restrooms off Mākena Rd. A popular shore-dive and kayak launch — fills with operators.
Big Beach (Oneloa, Mākena State Park)
Stunning to look at and walk, but the shorebreak is among the most dangerous in the world — admire it from the dry sand, not from in the water.

Powerful dumping shorebreak that breaks directly onto a steep sand face with NO trough — it can drive swimmers headfirst into the sand. Mākena/Big Beach LEADS the State of Hawaiʻi in spinal-cord injuries (Hawaiʻi Trauma Registry recorded 40 spinal injuries in the Mākena area, 33 at Big Beach, 2009–2017), with paralyzing neck and back injuries, plus broken bones and drownings. Lifeguards are present 8am–4:45pm but CANNOT prevent the shorebreak itself. Stay out of the water unless it is genuinely flat and you have strong ocean experience; never turn your back on the waves.
Three paved state-park lots off Mākena Rd, with restrooms. Gates open ~5am–7pm; arrive before 9am.
8am–4:45pm daily (Mākena State Park towers)
Little Beach (Puʻu ʻŌlaʻi)
A scenic hidden cove behind the Puʻu ʻŌlaʻi cinder cone — beautiful to visit, but no lifeguard, rocky entry and a real shorebreak mean you should only enter the water when it is calm.

No lifeguard and no vehicle access — reached only by a short, steep, slippery scramble over the lava bluff from the north end of Big Beach. Shorebreak and a strong offshore current can pound and pull swimmers; entry/exit is over rocks. Bodysurfers ride it, but it is not a casual swim beach. Note: the cove is an unofficial clothing-optional spot and public nudity is illegal on Maui — signage now prohibits nudity, alcohol and fires.
Park at the Mākena State Park (Big Beach) lots, then walk to the north end and climb the lava-rock trail (~0.3 mi).
Kanahā Beach Park

World-class kite/windsurf launch with a guarded swim section inside the reef. Swimmers must stay in the buoyed zone in front of the lifeguard tower; windsurfers/kiters launch after 11am, so swim early. Calmest for swimming early morning before trades. Avoid the water 72hrs after heavy rain (Kahului runoff).
Large paved county lot off Amala Pl, near Kahului airport. Restrooms, showers, shade trees.
H.A. Baldwin Beach Park

Lifeguarded, but the open beach has a hard dumping shorebreak — Maui leads the state in spinal injuries and Baldwin is a hotspot. Keep keiki in the calm reef-protected 'Baby Beach' cove at the far west end and ask the guard about conditions.

Lifeguarded, but the open main beach has a hard, dumping shorebreak that breaks directly on sand — a documented neck/spinal-injury hotspot ('there's a reason locals joke about a good chiropractor in Paia'). Do NOT bodysurf or stand in the shorebreak. Keep keiki only in the calm reef-protected 'Baby Beach' cove at the far west end (or 'Baldwin Cove' at the east end), and always check with the lifeguard about conditions before entering.
Two large paved lots off Hāna Hwy west of Pāʻia. Restrooms, showers, big pavilion.
Baby Beach (Pāʻia)

A long offshore reef makes a shallow, flat lagoon — a popular North Shore spot for toddlers. Best at mid-to-high tide; it goes very shallow and rocky at low tide, when sharp reef and exposed rock are exposure/cut hazards. No lifeguard, so watch kids closely and never leave them unattended. On a north swell, surf can wash over the reef into the pool.
Limited residential street parking off Pāʻia town. Walk-in access between houses — be respectful of the neighborhood.
No lifeguard — nearest at Baldwin
Spreckelsville Beach

A long, windy reef-fringed strand popular with windsurfers and kiters. A near-shore lava shelf, scattered reef shelves and trade-wind chop make it better for walking than swimming, and the constant kite/windsurf traffic is a hazard for anyone in the water. No lifeguard here — adults should treat it as a stronger-swimmer beach and stay out in rough trades.
Roadside/dirt access off Nonohe Pl and the Stable Rd end. No facilities.
No lifeguard — nearest at Kanahā or Baldwin
Sugar Cove Beach

A small sandy pocket at the east end of the Spreckelsville reef. Pretty and quiet, but reef shelves and trade-wind current make it a stronger-swimmer's beach with no lifeguard — scout before entering and stay out in rough trades.
Beach-access path beside the Sugar Cove condos off Nonohe Pl; very limited parking.
Tavares Beach

A locals' pocket beach between Pāʻia and Hoʻokipa with a small-wave surf break. No lifeguard and a past drowning in the shorebreak — fine for a stroll, but scout very carefully and do not swim alone if you enter.

No lifeguard and a DOCUMENTED DROWNING: a 69-year-old man was found dead face-down in the Tavares Bay shorebreak (Aug 2013). The reef, currents and shorebreak change fast and there is no one watching the water. Treat as a stroll/scout-only spot — do not enter unless conditions are clearly calm and you are a strong swimmer with a buddy; never swim alone here.
Small roadside pullout on Hāna Hwy just east of Pāʻia; short path down.
Kahului Harbor Beaches (Hoʻaloha / Kanahā Pond)

A convenient in-town shoreline by the commercial/cruise harbor — handy for a leg-stretch, not for swimming or snorkeling. Runoff, vessel traffic and murky water make this a non-swim stop; better beaches are minutes east.

This is a working commercial/cruise harbor, NOT a swimming beach — there is no safe ocean entry here. No lifeguard, harbor and vessel traffic, stream/urban runoff and poor water clarity. Highest water-quality advisory frequency on the island after rain (wait 72+ hours). Use it only as an in-town leg-stretch/photo stop; do not swim or snorkel.
Hoʻaloha Park lot beside the harbor in central Kahului. Easy paved access, restrooms.
Hoʻokipa Beach Park
Maui's iconic windsurf arena and a turtle-basking beach — incredible to watch, dangerous to swim.

Expert-only water. A rock and reef ledge rings a tiny pocket of sand, with strong rip currents, urchins, and heavy shorebreak — even with lifeguards present, swimming is not recommended. World-class winter waves (over ~20 ft on N swells) draw pro windsurfers and surfers only. Sudden building afternoon winds and shallow reef can quickly overpower novices; rogue waves possible even on calm-looking days. Watch the action from the bluff; do not enter unless you are a local-level wave sailor and very strong swimmer.
Paved lot and a scenic overlook on Hāna Hwy east of Pāʻia. Restrooms, showers. Sea turtles bask on the sand most afternoons — stay 10+ ft back.
8am–4:45pm daily (two towers)
Hāna Bay

The most protected, family-friendly water in the Hāna region — the breakwater and Kaʻuiki Head shelter the bay. Calm near the pier; current and rougher water build toward the open (NE/east) end, so keep kids near the pier and out of the open end.
Free county lot at the pier (Keawa Pl). Restrooms, showers, and Hāna Bay snack stand on site.
Mon–Sun 8am–4:45pm
Hāmoa Beach
A stunning cliff-backed crescent, but it faces open ocean — the shorebreak and a rip toward the rocks pull hard on a swell. Calm days only, stay near shore, and never turn your back on the water.

Open-ocean pocket beach with no reef and no lifeguard. Documented strong rip current that pulls swimmers toward the rocks at the ends, plus a hard dumping shorebreak on a swell. Hāmoa is repeatedly named among Maui's risky beaches for rescues. Enter only on a genuinely flat, calm day, stay close to shore, and never turn your back on the water — when in doubt, stay out.
Limited roadside parking on Haneoʻo Rd; steps lead down the cliff to the sand. Hotel-served but the beach is public.
Koki Beach
Come for the dramatic red-sand cliffs and the view of ʻĀlau Island — stay on the sand and out of the water. Locals do not swim here.

Persistent strong rip currents and a steep, dumping shorebreak on red/dark sand, fully exposed to open-ocean swell. No lifeguard. Multiple documented drownings (a man in Dec 2012; a swimmer in March 2022 pulled out and lost even in 'calm' conditions). This is NOT a swimming beach — stay on the sand.
Roadside dirt pullouts on Haneoʻo Rd. Easy to reach but no facilities.
Waiʻānapanapa Black Sand Beach (Paʻiloa)
One of the most photographed black-sand coves in Hawaiʻi — explore the lava tubes, sea arch, and coastal trail, but treat the water as look-don't-touch.

No protective reef, so the water deepens abruptly at the shoreline and a powerful, violent shorebreak funnels into a small lava-rock cove with strong currents and rip. No lifeguard. Swimmers have been swept onto the rocks. Portuguese man o' war are sometimes present. Treat as look-don't-touch; enter only on a genuinely flat day, if at all.

Waiʻānapanapa State Park — advance reservation required for non-residents ($5/person + $10/vehicle, gostateparks.hawaii.gov; no same-day). Paved lot, restrooms; short steep stairway to the black sand.
Kaihalulu (Red Sand Beach)

Famous for its deep-red cinder sand, but the access trail is the real hazard — it has been closed after recent storms/landslides and has caused airlift rescues and deaths. Do not attempt it, and never in wet conditions, with kids, or in flip-flops.

ACCESS IS THE PRIMARY KILLER: the only way in is a narrow, actively eroding cinder-cliff trail across a steep dropoff onto loose rock. At least a dozen serious falls since 2012, multiple helicopter airlifts (2023 and 2024), and the trail has been closed/advised-against after landslides and the 2026 Kona storms. The route crosses private land and Hawaiian burial grounds. The cove has a rock-gap opening to the open ocean where surge and rip can pull swimmers onto the reef. No lifeguard, no rescue access. Local groups ask visitors to stay away. Do not attempt.
No legal lot. Trail starts behind the Hāna community center / Hauʻoli Rd; the route crosses private land and Hawaiian burial grounds. Steep, crumbling, eroding, and dangerous — especially when wet.
Waimea Bay
Glassy and family-friendly in summer (May–Sep), but in winter this is a world-famous big-wave arena with deadly shorebreak and rip currents — obey the lifeguards and flags.

Summer it can be calm and swimmable, but from roughly Oct–Apr Waimea sees giant NW swell, a violent sand-bottom shorebreak that breaks necks, and strong rip currents. Never enter on a high-surf day. Jumping off the rock has killed and paralyzed people. Always check with the lifeguard tower.
County lot at Waimea Bay Beach Park fills by 9am; overflow roadside on Kamehameha Hwy is ticketed/towed.
8:00am–6:30pm daily (Honolulu Ocean Safety Tower 29; may extend during high surf)
ʻEhukai Beach (Banzai Pipeline)
The most famous and lethal wave on earth — a heavy reef barrel breaking in shallow water over sharp coral. A spectator beach for non-experts; do not paddle out unless you are an expert.

Pipeline/Backdoor breaks over a shallow, jagged reef just feet from shore. Even pro surfers die and are seriously injured here. The shorebreak and reef make this one of the deadliest surf spots in the world. Watch from the sand — non-experts must stay out of the water in any surf.
Small ʻEhukai Beach Park lot across from Sunset Beach Elementary; fills before dawn in winter. Roadside parking heavily enforced.
8:00am–6:30pm daily (Honolulu Ocean Safety Tower 26)
Sunset Beach

A long golden sand beach, gorgeous for sunset walks. Summer can be calm, but the famous winter break carries some of the strongest rip currents on the North Shore — the ‘Sunset rip’ has swept countless swimmers out.

Notorious for powerful, fast-moving rip currents (the ‘Sunset rip’) and large winter NW surf with hard shorebreak. Frequent rescues and drownings. Calm-looking days can still hide strong currents; check with lifeguards before entering and never swim in surf.
Sunset Beach Park lot and roadside pullouts along Kamehameha Hwy; very limited in winter surf season.
8:00am–6:30pm daily (Honolulu Ocean Safety Tower 25)
Haleʻiwa Aliʻi Beach Park

The most sheltered, family-oriented North Shore beach park and the safest local swim option, especially in summer — but it is still North Shore: respect the harbor channel current and never swim when winter surf is up. Keep kids in the guarded, sheltered pocket only.

Calmest of the major North Shore parks and the only reasonable family swim option, but it is still an open North Shore coast: a harbor channel current runs nearby and winter NW swell brings surf and rip risk. Swim only in the guarded, sheltered pocket, in calm conditions, and check with the lifeguard tower first.
Large free lot at Haleʻiwa Aliʻi Beach Park with restrooms and showers; generally easy parking.
8:00am–6:30pm daily (Honolulu Ocean Safety Tower 31)
Sharks Cove (Pūpūkea)

One of Oʻahu's best snorkel and tidepool spots — but ONLY in flat summer conditions. The rocky lava entry is treacherous and in any winter swell waves wash people onto the rocks; people have died here.

Part of the Pūpūkea Marine Life Conservation District — superb summer snorkeling, but the sharp lava-rock entry and exposure mean even moderate swell turns it deadly. Drownings and serious injuries occur when people enter on surf days (bodies recovered during high surf as recently as Dec 2023). Flat, calm summer mornings only; check the lifeguard and never enter with any wave action.
Roadside lot across Kamehameha Hwy by the Pūpūkea food trucks; busy mid-morning in summer.
New Honolulu Ocean Safety tower at Kapoʻo/Shark's Cove (Tower 28), blessed/opened ~Mar 2026; daily/seasonal coverage hours not yet officially published — confirm on-site [verify]
Laniākea Beach

Famous ‘Turtle Beach’ where green sea turtles (honu) bask on the sand — keep at least 10 feet back and never touch them. Treat it as having no lifeguard, the reef has sharp rocks, and winter brings strong currents, so this is mainly a turtle-viewing and photo stop.

Treat as no lifeguard. Reef and rock bottom plus strong winter currents (a strong rip forms in the west-side channel on swells) make swimming hazardous; it is a turtle-viewing beach, not a safe swim beach. Stay well back from basking honu (state and federal law) and beware fast traffic when crossing the highway from parking.
Dirt roadside pullout on the mauka side of Kamehameha Hwy; crossing the highway on foot is dangerous — use caution.

Treat as UNGUARDED. Honolulu's official tower list shows a Tower 30B at Laniākea, but multiple sources say there is no dependable on-site guard and the nearest reliable tower is Haleʻiwa Aliʻi — do not count on a lifeguard [verify]
Three Tables

Named for three flat reef tables that surface at low tide — excellent, easy summer snorkeling next to Sharks Cove. Like its neighbor, it is only safe on flat summer days; any swell makes the shallow reef dangerous. People die here every winter trying to swim during big swells.

Part of the Pūpūkea MLCD with no dedicated lifeguard at this spot. Shallow reef tables and a rocky entry make it dangerous in any swell — Oct–Apr north swells push 8–20ft surf into the bay and turn the entry into a washing machine; people drown here every winter. Flat, calm summer conditions only (roughly May–Sep). If white water is breaking on the outer reef, stay on the sand.
Same roadside lot as Sharks Cove on Kamehameha Hwy; short walk along the shore.
No dedicated lifeguard at Three Tables; nearest tower is the new Pūpūkea/Sharks Cove Tower 28 (a short walk away) — coverage not guaranteed at this spot [verify]
Chun's Reef

A gentler, mellow reef break popular with longboarders and learning surfers, and an OK summer snorkel at low surf — but treat it as having no lifeguard and the reef is shallow, so it still demands respect when waves are up.

Treat as no lifeguard and a shallow reef bottom. Often the ‘mellow’ North Shore option, but winter swell still produces strong currents and the reef causes injuries. Only suitable for confident swimmers/surfers in small, calm conditions.
Limited roadside pullouts along Kamehameha Hwy; small and often full.

Treat as UNGUARDED. Honolulu's official tower list shows a Tower 30A at Kawailoa/Chun's Reef, but coverage is not dependable — do not count on a lifeguard; nearest reliable tower is Haleʻiwa Aliʻi [verify]
Lanikai Beach

Postcard-calm and reef-protected at the shoreline behind the Mokulua islands, but there is no lifeguard and people have drowned in the channel out toward the Mokes. Stay in the shallows on a fair-weather day; do not paddle out to the islands unless you are an experienced, vested open-water paddler in calm conditions.

The shoreline itself is calm and reef-shielded, BUT there is no lifeguard and the water off Lanikai toward the Mokulua islets is deadly. At least four people have drowned in the waters off the Mokuluas since 1993, and in January 2024 Honolulu Ocean Safety pulled an unresponsive kayaker from the water roughly 100 yards off the beach and performed CPR. The channel and the swells that wrap around and clash between the two islands generate strong, deceptive currents that flip kayaks and exhaust swimmers; the Mokes are out of sight of the Kailua Beach lifeguard towers, so no one is watching and rescue is slow. Do not paddle, swim, or kayak to the Mokes without a PFD, strong open-water ability, and settled conditions.
No lot — narrow residential street parking only. Read posted signs carefully; tow zones enforced. Walk in via marked public beach-access paths between houses.
Kailua Beach Park
Guarded, gently shelving sand and usually mild — Hawaii's classic family bay. Trade-wind chop and a corner rip near the canal mouth pick up on windy afternoons, so swim near the tower.
Large county lot at the park; fills by mid-morning on weekends. Overflow along Kawailoa Rd.
8am–6:30pm daily
Kalama Beach
The calmer, less-crowded north end of Kailua Bay with its own guard tower (opened 2024). Shorebreak can stand up here on bigger trade swells, so keep kids near the lifeguard.
Small lot at Kalama Beach Park plus limited street parking; quieter than the main Kailua lot.
Waimānalo Bay Beach Park

Longest white-sand beach on Oʻahu and guarded — lifeguards often steer visitors here as a calmer alternative to Sandy Beach. But it is open ocean: the shorebreak dumps hard on bigger swells and bodyboarders get worked, so swim by a tower and respect a punchy day.
Shaded ironwood lots at Waimānalo Bay (Sherwoods/Hunānaniho) and Waimānalo Beach Park; ample but busy on weekends.
Bellows Field Beach Park

Soft sand and a popular beginner bodyboard shorebreak, but the lifeguard is only there during daytime weekend public-access hours — there is NO guard overnight or on weekdays even though the gate may be open until midnight. The same shorebreak that is fun on a small day turns punishing on a bigger swell — only swim when the tower is staffed and stay near it.
Gated military beach — public access only Fri noon to Sun midnight and on holidays. Paved lots inside the gate; bring ID. Can close for military training with no notice.
Guarded ONLY during weekend public access: roughly Fri noon–Sun midnight + holidays, lifeguard on duty in daylight only (≈10am–5pm). NO overnight or weekday lifeguard.
Kualoa Regional Park

Shallow, calm water inside Kāneʻohe Bay's barrier reef with Mokoliʻi (Chinaman's Hat) islet offshore — gentle for small kids at higher tide, but it goes very shallow and rocky at low tide, and the tide comes in fast if you wade out toward the islet.
Large free county lot at the regional park; rarely full on weekdays.
Daily 8am–6:30pm Memorial Day–Labor Day; weekends & holidays only off-season
Makapuʻu Beach Park

Spectacular cliffs, tide pools and the offshore islands make it a stunning stop — but the shorebreak injures inexperienced swimmers regularly. Enjoy the view; do not bodyboard here unless you have the skills.

Powerful, steep dumping shorebreak with no protecting reef — one of Oʻahu's most injury-prone bodyboard beaches. The wave breaks in inches of water directly onto sand and causes neck, back and shoulder (cervical-spine) injuries every year; strong rip currents pull out on bigger days. Guarded, but for expert bodyboarders/bodysurfers only — inexperienced swimmers and visitors should watch from shore. The city posts shorebreak warning signs at the access.
Paved lot off Kalanianaʻole Hwy below the lookout; fills on weekends.
Waikīkī Beach

Offshore reefs and breakwaters keep the swimming sections gentle most days; the famous beginner surf breaks (Canoes, Queens) sit just outside the swim zone. Watch for surfboard traffic and slippery reef shelves at low tide.
Paid garages at Kapiʻolani Park, Honolulu Zoo, and along Kalākaua Ave. Metered street parking fills early.
Ala Moana Beach Park

A wide offshore reef and a dredged channel make this the calmest, most kid-friendly swim on the south shore; the bottom drops off fast into the old 20–30ft boat channel, so keep weak swimmers and small kids in the shallow reef flat and away from the deep channel at the ʻewa end.
Large free lots inside the park along Ala Moana Blvd. Plentiful except on weekends.
Kaimana Beach (Sans Souci)

Quiet, locals-favorite end of Waikīkī below Diamond Head with calm reef-protected water; Hawaiian monk seals haul out and have pupped here, so by law give any resting seal at least 50 feet and never get between a seal and the water (a bite occurred here in 2021).
Free street parking along Kalākaua Ave by Kapiʻolani Park; paid lots nearby. Arrive before 9am on weekends.
Hanauma Bay
Watch the mandatory orientation video and snorkel only inside the inner reef; the outer reef, channels, Witch's Brew and Toilet Bowl are off-limits for good reason and have killed many visitors.

World-class snorkeling on the protected inner reef, but powerful rip currents run through the reef channels and out the bay mouth — at least ~51 drowning deaths recorded here since 1995. The 'Witch's Brew' cove, the back-reef toward the Toilet Bowl, and the cable-channel/Molokai Express current pull swimmers past the reef into the open bay. Stay inside the inner reef flat, never swim out over or past the reef, snorkel with a buddy, and obey the lifeguards' flagged areas.
Paid lot at the preserve; advance online reservations required for non-residents. Closed Mondays and Tuesdays; sell out within minutes.
6:45am–4:00pm; entry closes 1:30pm; closed Mon & Tue
Sandy Beach
Stunning to watch the bodysurfers and the nearby blowhole, but do not go in the water unless you have local-level shorebreak skill — this beach breaks necks, even when the waves look small.

The most dangerous shorebreak on Oʻahu and reportedly the highest neck/back-injury beach in the United States ('Break Neck Beach'). A steep sand-bottom drop-off forces waves to pitch and slam riders headfirst onto hard-packed sand — most spinal injuries happen on SMALL days, not big ones, and rip currents and undertow appear as surf builds. Lifeguards make rescues at roughly 2.5x/day and treat every rescue as a potential spinal injury. Only experienced bodysurfers/bodyboarders should enter, and only after checking with lifeguards. Visitors should stay out of the water.
Free lot across Kalanianaʻole Hwy and roadside pullouts. Easy access right off the road.
China Walls (Koko Kai)
Spectacular for sunset photos from well back on the cliff; never stand near the water's edge or enter the ocean — a single set can sweep you in, and no lifeguard is watching.

A lava cliff shelf, NOT a swimming beach, and one of the most dangerous spots on Oʻahu — rescues happen frequently, especially in the April–October south-swell season. Large sets sweep without warning along the rock and pull people off the ledge into deep water against the cliff, with no easy exit and no lifeguard. Cliff-jumpers are routinely slammed on the rocks and several people have drowned. Honolulu Ocean Safety urges people not to swim or jump here.
Limited residential street parking in Portlock (Koko Kai Pl); be respectful of the neighborhood. Short walk down to the lava shelf.
Ko Olina Lagoons
Four man-made, breakwater-protected lagoons — the calmest, most kid-safe water on the Leeward coast. No city lifeguards: the resort posts 'swim at your own risk,' so watch your own kids closely.
Four free public lots (one per lagoon), but they fill by mid-morning — arrive before 9am. Public access is required by law despite the resort setting.
No city lifeguard — private resort, swim at own risk
Pōkaʻī Bay Beach Park
A breakwater shelters the bay, making it the calmest lifeguarded swim on the Waianae coast — genuinely safe for kids most of the year. Honor that you are a guest in a tight-knit local community.
Free county lot at Pōkaʻī Bay Beach Park on Bayview St. Generally easy parking on weekdays.
Mākaha Beach

A legendary surf beach — gentle and swimmable in calm summer, but big west and northwest swells (mainly fall–winter) build powerful waves, a dumping shorebreak, and rip currents. Check with the lifeguards before entering and always swim near the tower.

Powerful surf beach. Calm and swimmable only on flat summer days; west and northwest swells (mainly fall–winter, waves to 25ft off Makaha Point) build a strong dumping shorebreak, heavy backwash, rip currents, and a shallow reef. Documented rescues and drownings on the Makaha–Pokai stretch. Lifeguarded (Towers 47A/47B) — never enter without checking with the guards, and only swim directly in front of a staffed tower.
Free lot and roadside parking along Farrington Hwy fronting the beach.
Māʻili Beach Park
A long sandy park with big lawns and two lifeguard towers. Sandbars shift and shorebreak can be sharp when swell is up — swim in front of a staffed tower and ask about the day's current.

Long open west-facing beach exposed to west/northwest swell. Shifting sandbars and a sharp dumping shorebreak when swell is up, with rip currents; drownings are documented along the Maili stretch of the Waianae coast. Two lifeguard towers (43A/43B) — only swim directly in front of a staffed tower and ask about the day's current before entering.
Long county beach park with multiple free lots and ample roadside parking on Farrington Hwy.
Nānākuli Beach Park
A community beach park with a lifeguard tower and decent summer snorkeling on the calm days. Winter and big-swell days bring a dumping shorebreak — swim near the tower and check conditions first.

Strong shorebreak that can dump even on summer days, and high surf with strong currents in winter. Drownings are documented on the Nanakuli stretch of the Waianae coast. Lifeguarded (Tower 41, Kalanianaʻole Beach Park) — swim only directly in front of a staffed tower and check conditions first; snorkel only on flat, calm days.
Free county lot at Kalanianaʻole Beach Park (Nānākuli). Easy parking most days.
Electric Beach (Kahe Point)

The power-plant warm-water outflow draws a remarkable concentration of fish and turtles, making it one of the Leeward coast's best snorkels — but it is a ~200-yard open-water swim over a rocky entry with real currents, and a snorkeler drowned here in 2023. Go only on calm days, with a buddy and a dive flag, and talk to the lifeguard first.

Snorkel-only site with NO safe swim entry: a rocky lava-bench shore and an unavoidable ~200-yard open-water swim out to the power-plant outflow pipes, with real currents. A snorkeler drowned here in 2023 (before the tower existed) and it is a recognized rescue hot spot; tour groups concentrate inexperienced snorkelers here. A lifeguard tower now exists but the outflow swim is well offshore — go ONLY on flat, calm days, with a buddy and a dive flag, and check in with the lifeguard first.
Small gravel lot at Kahe Point Beach Park across Farrington Hwy from the power plant. Cross the highway carefully.
Lifeguard Tower 40 (opened Aug 2023). Honolulu tower-locations list shows 8am–6:30pm daily; original city announcement said 9am–5:30pm — confirm current hours before relying on a guard.
Yokohama Bay (Keawaʻula)
The last beach before Kaʻena Point — stunning and wild. Treat it as a photography and sunset spot, not a swim spot, unless the ocean is dead flat.

Remote beach with a steep, dumping shorebreak, strong currents, and a rocky bottom. There is a lifeguard tower (Tower 50) at the very end of the road, but it is frequently understaffed or unstaffed and you must not count on a guard being present. Multiple deaths have occurred in this area, including two 17-year-old fishermen swept off the rocks near here in October 2025. Enter only on a flat, calm summer day, near a staffed tower; in any swell, stay on the sand. Treat surrounding rocky points as no-go in any surf.
End-of-the-road dirt and paved parking at Keawaʻula / Kaena Point State Park. No services. Car break-ins reported — leave nothing in the car.
Tower 50 listed 8am–6:30pm but remote and often unstaffed — do not rely on it
Kahaluʻu Beach Park

Best beginner snorkel on the island — green sea turtles graze the reef. But this is the busiest rescue beach in Kona: stay inside the bay, avoid the north-end rip channel ('the chute') that pulls swimmers out to sea, and never turn your back on the surf. Watch the lifeguard's flags.

County lifeguards and Fire Dept. rescue personnel make MORE rescues here than at any other beach in Kona. A powerful rip current ('the chute') runs north from the Kuʻemanu Heiau end along the rocks and out to sea; swimmers who fight it have drowned from exhaustion. Stay inside the reef-enclosed bay, keep clear of the north end, and obey lifeguard flags. Reef rock and surge can also injure entries/exits.
County lot off Aliʻi Dr. Fills early — arrive before 9am. Restrooms and showers on site.
Mon–Sun ~9:30am–4:45pm per oceansafety.hawaii.gov official list (draft's 8:30–4:30 was WRONG)
Laʻaloa Beach (Magic Sands / White Sands)
Beautiful pocket beach but the shorebreak is no joke — boogie-boarders and waders get hurt here regularly, including neck and spine injuries. Swim only when flat; obey the lifeguard.

Severe seasonal shorebreak that dumps directly onto a steep sand face — neck, back and shoulder injuries are common (locally nicknamed 'Tragic Slams'), one of Hawaiʻi's worst beaches for spinal/neck injuries. Sand washes away entirely in winter swell (hence 'Magic'/'Disappearing' Sands). Powerful backwash and rip currents form fast; lifeguards report near-daily rescues even on calm summer days. Enter only on calm days, never turn your back on the waves, and obey the lifeguard.
Small lot and roadside on Aliʻi Dr. Limited — fills fast.
Kua Bay (Maniniʻōwali)

Postcard white sand and turquoise water in summer. In winter the shorebreak turns punishing and the sand strips away. Do not assume a lifeguard is on duty — check conditions before entering and stay out when surf is up.

Heavy seasonal shorebreak that turns punishing in winter, plus high surf and strong currents — official condition data flags heavy shore break, high surf and strong currents ('swim at your own risk'). In winter the sand strips away and the cove can be cut off; nearest fire/medical backup historically 15–20 min away. Lifeguard staffing is NOT confirmed on the current state list (see notes) — do not assume a guard is in the tower. Check flags/conditions and enter only on calm summer days.
Paved lot in Kekaha Kai State Park (Maniniʻōwali). Gate hours apply; lot fills mid-morning.

County funded a lifeguard tower here in July 2019 and lifeguards have been reported on duty during the day, BUT Kua Bay is NOT on the current oceansafety.hawaii.gov guarded list — staffing/hours UNCONFIRMED [verify]
Makalawena Beach

One of the island's most stunning undeveloped white-sand beaches, reached only on foot. No lifeguard and remote — swim conservatively, never alone, and stay out of the water with any winter swell because help is far away.

Remote, unguarded white-sand beach reached only on foot (~20–30 min hike over lava) or rough 4WD. No lifeguard, no facilities, and nearest rescue is far away. Currents can be strong and surf rough, especially with winter swell; help is not close. Swim conservatively, never alone, and stay out when surf is up.
No direct parking. Park at Mahaiʻula (Kekaha Kai State Park) and walk ~20–30 min over lava, or 4WD a rough track. Bring water — no facilities.
Mahaiʻula Beach (Kekaha Kai State Park)
Quiet salt-and-pepper sand beach with shade trees and good summer snorkeling. No lifeguard — watch for shorebreak and currents when surf is up, and stay close to shore.

No lifeguard anywhere in Kekaha Kai State Park. Generally calmer than Kua Bay in summer, but shorebreak and currents pick up when surf is up, and rescue response is slow on this remote leeward coast. Watch conditions, stay close to shore, and stay out with winter swell.
Rough 1.5-mile gravel road into Kekaha Kai State Park (passable for most cars slowly). Gate closes; check posted hours. No drinking water.
Hōnaunau Bay (Two Step)

The island's premier shore-dive and snorkel — but there is no sand and no lifeguard, and the lava-ledge entry ('Two Step') turns dangerous with any surge. Go only on calm mornings, enter/exit between swell sets, and skip it entirely if the bay is moving.

No sand and NO lifeguard — entry/exit is off two lava ledges directly into deep water. When any surge or swell is running, the ledge entry becomes dangerous: surge can slam you onto the rock and exits can be impossible. Only experienced swimmers/snorkelers should enter, and only in calm morning conditions. Time exits between sets; sea urchins lurk in the ledge holes.
Very limited. Small county lot and roadside; most park at Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau NHP and walk. Arrive early.
Kamakahonu Beach (Kailua Pier / King Kam)

Tiny, very calm pocket of sand beside the pier — the safest swim in Kailua-Kona town and great for small kids. No lifeguard, and it's busy with canoe paddlers and pier/boat traffic, so keep kids close and stay clear of the channel.
Public lot near Kailua Pier in Kailua-Kona town; metered/limited. Walkable from downtown.
Kekaha Kai State Park (Mahaiʻula–Makalawena area; draft 'Manini Beach' label is incorrect)

A remote stretch of leeward coast with white and salt-and-pepper sand. No lifeguard anywhere in the park — stay close to shore and respect winter swell. (This is the broader park between Mahaiʻula and Makalawena.)

No lifeguard anywhere in Kekaha Kai State Park. Remote leeward shoreline with white and salt-and-pepper sand; shorebreak and currents strengthen with surf and rescue is slow. Stay close to shore and respect winter swell. NOTE: this is a duplicate/umbrella entry that geographically overlaps the Mahaiʻula and Makalawena records.
Access via the Kekaha Kai State Park gravel road off Highway 19; gate hours posted. No facilities/water — bring your own.
Hāpuna Beach

Half-mile of white sand and the island's best all-around swimming beach in calm summer conditions — but it leads Hawaiʻi in shorebreak spinal injuries. The gentler southern end is safer. Lifeguarded daily; on any swell the dumping shorebreak can slam you onto a flat sand shelf, so check the flags and ask the tower before going in.

Lifeguarded daily, but a steep, dumping shorebreak makes this the state's leading beach for spinal-cord/neck injuries (locally called 'Broke Neck Beach'; 18+ documented spinal injuries, DOH-flagged alongside Sandy Beach and Mākena). Winter and big-NW-swell days bring powerful shorebreak and rip currents. Never dive or turn your back on the wave at the shorebreak; check the flags and ask the tower before entering.
State park lot off Hwy 19. $5/person entry + $10 parking fee for non-residents. Fills by mid-morning in winter.
9:30am–4:45pm daily
Kaunaʻoa Beach (Mauna Kea)

A perfect crescent fronting the Mauna Kea Beach Hotel — calm and family-friendly in summer. No lifeguard, and the same NW winter swell that hits Hāpuna builds a pounding shorebreak and rip currents here, so judge conditions yourself before entering and stay out when the surf is up.

No lifeguard. Calm and family-friendly in summer, but in winter high surf brings a pounding shorebreak and strong rip currents with no one watching. Judge conditions yourself; do not enter when surf is up.
Public access through Mauna Kea Beach Hotel — a limited number of free public parking passes issued daily at the gate. Arrive early; they run out.
Samuel M. Spencer Beach Park

The calmest, most protected swimming on the Kohala coast — an offshore reef knocks the swell down, making it the go-to for young kids and first-time snorkelers. Lifeguarded daily per the state list, though some travel sites report weekends/holidays only — if in doubt, treat midweek as unguarded and check the tower.
County park lot off Hwy 270 near Puʻukoholā Heiau. Usually space available. Restrooms, showers, camping.
Waialea Bay (Beach 69)

Locals call it Beach 69 for the old telephone pole marker. Reef on both ends makes it one of the best easy snorkels in Kohala on calm summer mornings. No lifeguard — calm most mornings, but check for swell on the open-water side and expect murkier water after rain from the intermittent stream.

No lifeguard. Calm, reef-protected snorkeling most summer mornings, but winter surf erodes the beach and builds surf on the open-water side, and an intermittent stream can drop visibility. Stay near the protected reef ends and check for swell before swimming out.
State park lot off Puako Beach Dr (look for utility pole 69). Small — arrive before 9am on weekends.
Mauʻumae Beach

A hidden pocket beach reached by a short coastal trail — quiet and beautiful, calm only on flat summer days. No lifeguard and no easy exit if the surf is up, with slow emergency response this far out, so treat it as a swim-at-your-own-risk spot and skip the water when there's any swell.

No lifeguard and no quick rescue access — remote pocket beach reached only by a 10-15 min trail, with no facilities and slow emergency response. Calm only on flat summer days; there is no easy, safe exit if the surf comes up. Swim at your own risk, never alone.
Roadside near the Mauna Kea Resort residential gate (beach pass required at the gate), then a 10-15 min trail down. No facilities.
Kīholo Bay

A turquoise spring-fed bay where green sea turtles rest on the lava — stunning and worth the rough drive. But there is no lifeguard, no cell service, and tiger sharks are reported near the murky river mouths, so keep swimming to the calm brackish lagoon, skip the murky open water entirely, and never go in alone. Stay 10ft from turtles (it's the law).

No lifeguard, remote, and no cell service — emergency help is far away. Freshwater springs make the water cold and murky, and tiger sharks are documented near the river/spring mouths where visibility is low; open-bay currents add risk. The calm brackish lagoon is the safest swim; do not swim in the murky open bay, and never alone.
Unmarked gravel road makai between mile markers 82 and 83 on Hwy 19; rough but passable for a careful 2WD. No facilities, no cell service.
Pololū Valley Beach

One of the most spectacular viewpoints on the island. The black-sand beach is for walking and photos only — the water has strong currents and shorebreak in every season, no lifeguard, and a long emergency response, so stay out of the ocean entirely.

Powerful shorebreak and strong year-round rip currents on an exposed, unsheltered black-sand beach at the bottom of a steep cliff trail. No lifeguard, 30+ minute emergency response, and multiple documented drownings; even local residents and rescue divers do not enter the water here. Hike in for the views — do not swim.
Lot at the end of Hwy 270 in Kapaʻau. Steep 15-20 min switchback trail down to the beach.
Richardson Ocean Park

Best snorkel on the Hilo side — cold freshwater springs feed a cove sheltered behind a black-rock barrier, and green sea turtles rest here (stay 10 ft back). Calm on normal days, but during high surf strong currents and rip can develop and the park is closed; always check with the lifeguard before entering.

Sheltered and lifeguarded, but not risk-free: a swimmer drowned here in 2005 after being overcome by waves and current, and the County closes the park during high-surf events when rip currents form. Heed lifeguard guidance and stay out during posted high surf.
Small lot off Kalanianaʻole Ave, 6 mi east of Hilo. Fills fast on weekends — arrive early.
Carlsmith Beach Park (Four Mile)

Lava-rock breakwater forms a calm lagoon — turtles graze the inner pools and it's gentle enough for kids on normal days. Entry is over rock, not sand, so wear reef shoes. Closed during high surf, when currents pick up; check the lifeguard.

Calm and lifeguarded most days, but the County closes Carlsmith during high-surf events when strong currents run the shoreline. Rocky entry; mind footing and check conditions with the lifeguard before entering.
Free lot on Kalanianaʻole Ave at the 4-mile marker (hence 'Four Mile'). Grassy lawn, restrooms, showers.
Leleiwi Beach Park (Waiʻuli)

Rocky tidepool coastline with sheltered inlets — good snorkeling when the surf is down, but entry is over lava with no sand beach, so it suits confident swimmers over young kids. Closed during high surf; check the lifeguard.

Lava-rock entry with no sand beach; protective rock wall breaks most current but the County closes Leleiwi during high-surf events when currents run hard. Confident swimmers only; not for young children. Verify conditions with the lifeguard.
Lot off Kalanianaʻole Ave near road's end in Keaukaha. Restrooms and showers.
Onekahakaha Beach Park

A boulder-walled wading pool makes this the safest spot for toddlers near Hilo. Stay inside the protected pool — the open ocean side past the rocks has strong current, where past drownings have happened. Closed during high surf.

The walled keiki pool is the safest Hilo spot for small children, but the open-ocean side past the rocks has strong current where drownings/near-drownings occurred before lifeguards were posted. Stay inside the pool; park closes during high surf.
Free lot off Onekahakaha Rd, closest beach park to Hilo town. Lawns, restrooms, showers.
Honoliʻi Beach Park

The best-known surf break on the Hilo side — not a swim beach. Rocky bottom, rip currents, a fast-changing river mouth, and a quick drop-off. Watch the surfers from the bluff; stay out of the water unless you surf at a local level.

Premier Hilo surf break, not a swimming beach. Rocky bottom, common rip currents, and a river mouth whose flow can surge without warning. The nearshore bottom drops off fast and shorebreak pounds the rivermouth cobble. Lifeguarded during the day, but enter the water only if you surf at a local-equivalent level.
Roadside on Kahoa St, ~2 mi N of Hilo. Stairs down to the cove.
Pohoiki (Isaac Hale Beach Park)

The Big Island's youngest black-sand beach, born from the 2018 Kīlauea eruption. Lava boulders line the waterline and a hard shorebreak with strong currents runs the sand — go for the geology and the warm volcanic ponds, not for swimming. Do not count on a lifeguard.

Brand-new (2018 lava) black-sand beach with a dangerous shorebreak and strong currents along the sand. Lava boulders make ocean entry hard even on calm days. This is NOT a swimming beach. Lifeguard coverage is not on the official State list and any tower is staffed only seasonally — do not rely on a guard being present. The DOH also warns against entering the warm geothermal ponds with any open wound (bacterial-infection risk).
Gravel lot at the end of Hwy 137 (Pohoiki Rd) in lower Puna. Boat ramp, restrooms.
No lifeguard confirmed on the official list — any tower coverage is seasonal/unverified
Kehena Beach

A striking secluded black-sand cove (clothing-optional), but it faces the open ocean with no protection. Beautiful from the sand — treat the water as look-don't-touch unless it is dead calm, and even then conditions can turn fast.

Fully exposed to open-ocean swell with a brutal shorebreak and rip currents/undertow that have caused MULTIPLE drownings (documented deaths 2017, 2019, 2022, 2024). No lifeguard, limited cell service, and a steep cliff trail that makes rescue slow — bystanders have been unable to reach victims. Enter only in genuinely calm conditions, never alone; safest treated as look-don't-touch.
Roadside pullout on Hwy 137 near mile marker 19. Steep, slick 5-min trail down the cliff.
Punaluʻu Black Sand Beach

The island's most famous black-sand beach and a hawksbill/green-turtle haul-out — stay 10+ ft back, never touch them. Cold freshwater springs and a rip near the boat ramp make swimming risky even though the park is staffed; most visitors come to photograph turtles, not swim.

Despite a lifeguard tower at the park, the water here is hazardous: a strong rip runs out the boat channel/ramp on the north/northeast side, cold offshore freshwater springs cause sudden temperature shock, and high surf is common. A swimmer drowned here (Puna man, Sept 2014). Most visitors come to photograph turtles, not swim. Check with lifeguards and the flag before any water entry; do not swim near the boat ramp.
Free county lot off Hwy 11 at Punaluʻu (between mile markers 55-56, near Pāhala/Nāʻālehu). Restrooms and picnic pavilions on site.
Mon-Sun ~9:30am-4:45pm (Hawaiʻi County Ocean Safety tower at the park; some sources report 8:30am-5pm — VERIFY current hours before relying on coverage)
Papakōlea Green Sand Beach (Mahana Bay)
One of only a handful of green-sand beaches on Earth — spectacular to see, but treat it as a viewpoint, not a swim beach.

Remote olivine-sand cove inside a collapsed cinder cone with no lifeguard, no shade, and no rescue. The bay opens to the open South-Point swell window; strong wrap-around currents are hard to spot, waves can break directly onto the steep cobble shore, and the only exit is a ~2.5-mi cliff-edge hike. Visitor drowning/distress reports exist. Treat as a viewpoint, not a swim beach — if you enter at all, only on a genuinely flat day, never alone, and stay close to shore.
Dirt lot at end of South Point Rd; ~2.5 mi each way on foot (4WD route is rutted and tears up rentals — locals run unofficial paid shuttles).
Ka Lae (South Point)
Come for the wind farm, the fishing canoe moorings, and the raw edge-of-the-world view — do not jump from the cliffs or enter the water.

The southernmost point of the USA — lava cliffs over deep open ocean, NOT a swimming beach. The powerful converging 'Halaea Current' sweeps straight out to sea with nothing to stop you. Cliff-jumping from the old wooden platforms has repeatedly killed and badly injured people — at least four deaths in the six years to 2024 plus a Dec 2025 visitor fatality. If a current takes you, rescue is unlikely. Do not jump and do not enter the water.
Paved-then-rough road to cliff edge; informal dirt parking. No facilities, no shade.
Kaʻalualu Bay
A backcountry fishing and camping bay for the well-prepared only — go with a local who knows the road, tell someone your plan, and treat the water as dangerous.

Very remote, road-less bay reached only by a long, rough 4WD track (sources describe up to ~6.5 mi one way). No lifeguard, no reliable cell coverage, no facilities, and no help if anything goes wrong. Rocky entry and exposed currents; a Nāʻālehu man drowned here in Dec 2014. Treat any water entry as fully self-rescue.
No formal parking; long, rough 4WD-only track off the South Point / Kaʻalualu-Waiōhinu area (reports up to ~6.5 mi one way). High-clearance vehicle and self-sufficiency required.
Whittington Beach Park (Honuʻapo)

A grassy county park with old sugar-landing ruins and rich tidepools rather than a swim beach — turtles and fish gather in the protected inlet, but the rocky shore and surge make it a look-and-explore spot, not a swimming one.

A rocky lava shoreline on Honuʻapo Bay, NOT a sand swimming beach, with no lifeguard. Rough surf, strong currents, and rocks make the open shoreline dangerous for swimming; surge can sweep the rocks and tidepools. Stay to the sheltered tidepools/old fishponds and treat the open water as a no-swim zone.
Free county park lot off Hwy 11 near Honuʻapo (94-4995 Mamalahoa Hwy, Nāʻālehu). Restrooms, pavilions, camping by permit.
Honuʻapo Bay (Honuʻapo Estuary)

A restored fishpond-and-wetland preserve where turtles bask and shorebirds feed — beautiful coastal walking and birding, but rocky shoreline and ocean surge mean it is for exploring on foot, not getting in the water.

A restored fishpond/wetland estuary preserve on Honuʻapo Bay with a rocky shoreline and no lifeguard — for coastal walking and birding, not swimming. Ocean surge and currents along the rocks, combined with stream/estuary mixing, make water entry hazardous. Explore on foot; do not swim.
Gravel lot at the Honuʻapo (Kaʻū Coast) county/land-trust preserve off Hwy 11, just south of Whittington. No services.
